title: After a key new way of life is acquired, many divergent forms arise quickly

fields.label: Label
fields.value: After a key new way of life is acquired, many divergent forms arise quickly

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Adapting an organism to a new and peculiar way of life such as flight may take a long time, but once a few species have gained that advantage, many divergent forms can be produced in a comparatively short time and spread widely.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: but that when this had been effected, and a few species had thus acquired a great advantage over other organisms, a comparatively short time would be necessary to produce many divergent forms, which would be able to spread rapidly and widely throughout the world.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IX, “On the Imperfection of the Geological Record”; section “On the sudden appearance of groups of species”. Scope: groups that acquire a novel mode of life (e.g. flying animals)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch09-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.56

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Comparative phylogenetic and fossil analyses can test restricted examples such as flight. Available data and causal identification are too uneven for the broad mechanism as stated.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Identify independently evolved ecological innovations, estimate waiting time to acquisition, subsequent diversification rates, disparity, and geographic spread, and compare these with sister groups lacking the innovation. Support requires consistently elevated post-innovation radiation and dispersal after a longer acquisition interval.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Innovation, diversification, and dispersal are confounded with environment and preservation.

A 'peculiar way of life' and 'comparatively short' require subjective thresholds.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.58
discriminating power: 0.43
analysis feasibility: 0.58
data adequacy: 0.45
data existence: 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fossil occurrences and published timetrees can time the radiations of bats, birds, and pterosaurs, which is the testable core for a few cases. The preceding long evolution of the habit is mostly unrecorded, so that half of the statement stays thin. Results for flight do not automatically extend to every new way of life.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For clades that gained a novel habit such as flight, measure the time from the oldest stem fossil to the appearance of many divergent, geographically widespread subclades. A long prelude and then a short global radiation would support the claim; diversification spread evenly across the whole interval would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The acquisition of the new habit itself is rarely fossilized, so the long prelude is weakly constrained.

Comparatively short needs an external yardstick, and clock dates and fossil dates often disagree.

Only a few novel habits have both a fossil origin and a resolved radiation.
